text: Daniel Burnham, a Chicago architect, was the chief of construction.
He oversaw nearly two hundred buildings and the army of workers who raised them.
To pick the look of the main halls, he chose ten of the country's leading firms, five from Chicago and five from the East, so the fair would feel national.
Richard Morris Hunt of New York drew the Administration Building.
Charles McKim's firm did the Agriculture Building.
Burnham gave them one shared rule.
Their cornices would meet at a single height, sixty feet, and they would all be white.
Frederick Law Olmsted, who had laid out New York's Central Park, took the swampy ground and turned it into lagoons and a wooded island.
What Olmsted built was a stage.
What Burnham built was the set.
At the center stood the Court of Honor, a ring of enormous halls finished in white over wood and a fiber called staff.
They were not marble.
They were plaster and burlap and lath, made to photograph like stone.
The largest of them, the Manufactures and Liberal Arts Building, covered nearly thirty-two acres under one roof, the biggest building in the world at the time.
Crews worked through a brutal Chicago winter to raise it all on a deadline, and the fair's own medical bureau later counted thirty-two deaths during construction.
Almost the only hall that broke the white scheme was Louis Sullivan's Transportation Building, off to one side, with colored walls and a great arched Golden Door.
Sullivan thought the rest of it was a mistake.
He wrote later that the classical fashion the fair made popular had set American architecture back by half a century.
At night the basin was strung with electric light, thousands of bulbs at once, in a decade when most American homes still burned gas or oil.
People started calling it the White City.
